utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody [French on English channel]. Are we hearing French? Now it's okay. There's one ruling to be issued orally today. On 31st May 2010, the accused filed the motion to exclude testimony of Richard Philipps. He requested the Chamber to exclude Richard Philipps' testimony on the basis that it would not be of any assistance to the Chamber at this stage of the proceedings. The Prosecution filed its response on 2nd June 2010. The Chamber has considered the parties' submission and will now issue its decision thereon. The accused merely asserts that Philipps' evidence will not assist the Chamber in the determination of the issues of this case but it does not provide any basis for this assertion. However, he is charged with the responsibility for crimes that allegedly were committed in Sarajevo by members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, a unit of the Bosnian VRS of which he is said to have been the supreme commander. According to the Prosecution, Philipps will provide evidence concerning the command and reporting structures of the SRK. Based on its review of Mr. Philipps' report, diagrams and amalgamated statements, the Chamber is satisfied that his evidence will indeed be of some assistance to the Chamber. Therefore, the Chamber denies the accused's motion. Having said that, we are coming to the overall time for cross-examination on the part of the accused. As I said yesterday that we would come to the issue again, so as regards the time remaining for Mr. Karadzic's crosses examination of Dr. Donia, having observed the -- his conduct of cross-examination so far, we are not satisfied that Mr. Karadzic has used his time efficiently in compliance with the Court's guidance. In particular, at the outset the Chamber made it clear that his estimated time of 40 hours was not reasonable. He referred back to it yesterday when asked how much time he had for remaining time. He used often, usually often, open questions, making comments, statements, reading out unnecessary parts of all the documents. So at this time, the Chamber has decided to require him to conclude his cross-examination of Dr. Donia by tomorrow. So by tomorrow, he will have had more than 18 hours, which the Chamber finds more than sufficient. And as regards Mr. Philipps, the Chamber notes that he has asked for 20 hours for cross-examination of Mr. Philipps. The Chamber also finds this estimation patently unreasonable, particularly as the accused sees no benefit for the Chamber of Mr. Philipps' evidence pursuant to his motion. Moreover, the Chamber notes that Mr. Philipps' evidence will be very specific, limited to the command and reporting structures of the SRK, and it is unable to see how the accused could need anywhere near the 20 hours he has estimated for cross-examination. Therefore, the Chamber expects the accused to take no longer than five hours for his cross-examination of Richard Philipps. That said, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to say that I'm not protected enough from the evasive answers of the witness and his partiality. Therefore, this will not be sufficient. Please reconsider your decision in view of how the proceedings evolve today, because the trial will certainly suffer if this witness is not cross-examined on all the facts that he dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have two full days, and get on with it, and we'll see at the end of -- yes, we'll see at the end of these sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, we apologise for your inconvenience. There was something we needed to discuss in your absence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all. Could I please have 1D181 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, did you know towards the end of August we had reached an agreement to the effect that all three ruling parties together follow all developments and do their best to reduce political tensions? You have before you -- well, I believe there's a translation too. No, there's no translation. All right. You want me to read this out to you, at least the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "To all Municipal Boards of the SDS and to the regional --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry I didn't rise earlier. 65 ter 14837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That will be faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see here, Mr. Donia -- actually, I can read this. This is the Serbian version, what we see right now. The first paragraph. I would like to draw your attention to the first paragraph. The rest is not important for this particular issue. I can't see the translation. Then I'll have to read it nevertheless: "I hereby inform you that I have reached agreement with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic." Here it is. Here it is, "President of the Party of Democratic Action and Mr. Stjepan Kljujic president of the Croatian democratic community that these three political parties establish observer groups tasked with monitoring all developments in their respect communities --" Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have English translation now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this from some other source? Did you know about these joint commissions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've also never seen the -- I've never seen the agreement. If there's a written agreement, I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I say here that we have reached an agreement. It's not that we signed an agreement. We have reached agreement. We have accommodated our views. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D39.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Donia, do you know that after this crisis, when Izetbegovic withdrew from the historic agreement, that then, on the 11th of September we reached a new milestone in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that we then passed certain conclusions in the Assembly that are now going to appear before you. Are you aware of these conclusions of the 11th of September?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just may I -- when you say "we," did you mean the SDS since you, yourself, were not a member of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We, I mean the joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time it was still the joint Assembly, because there was still a one and only Bosnia, a united Bosnia. That's the only Assembly there was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I know you were not a member of that Assembly, but you're saying "we," and so I take it you mean the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All parties. All parties in the Assembly. Have a look at these conclusions. Would I like to draw your attention to the last one. Actually, the penultimate one. "The Assembly is committed to finding," et cetera. You see that here we reached agreement that there has to be a political solution, that all proposals are legitimate and that no force would be resorted to and that no one would impose anything upon anybody else. Were you aware of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D265, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D40, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know what the Party of Democratic Action was doing at this very same time? Did you study their activity at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've studied their -- their general position and activities, but I certainly haven't followed it on a day-by-day basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document before you? You can read our language, but there is a translation too. I see that. On the 26th of September it was received, and the Party of Democratic Action, on the 20th of September, had ordered the monitoring of all activities and movements, primarily of the Yugoslav People's Army. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I need just a minute to look at this if I may. Okay. I see that they are simply monitoring developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 of this document. In English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this instructions as to how all of this should be monitored and how one should act in general? Can you see all of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the -- I think the rationale here is contained in the third -- third paragraph here where they are -- where the SDS is discussing this movement of civilian vehicles which had been in the near recent past transporting both personnel and weapons from across Bosnian territory. It seems to me to be the point of concern that probably generated this request for monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that this was legal activity? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was -- I don't know whether the transport of troops and weapons in civilian automobiles was -- was legal or not, and I'm not sure that the -- the monitoring itself -- I wouldn't think it's illegal but don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that three weeks before that we had passed a decision that we should monitor together all phenomena that may be of relevance? Remember the first document that I showed you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at that document again, but it didn't -- as I recall it, it didn't seem to preclude other activities by the parties. It was -- I interpreted that first document as to be a reference to efforts to work out conflicts in the inter-party agreements and other personnel issues, but I wasn't there, wasn't a party to it, so I'm not really certain what was actually intended in those passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're right. The first one said that all three parties should follow social developments in order to reduce tensions, whereas this is secret monitoring of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D266, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D41.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Donia, that the OSCE established a Crisis Staff for monitoring developments in Yugoslavia and that Germany, in Bonn, had established a Crisis Staff for monitoring developments in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very much doubt that the OSCE used the word "Crisis Staff," but I'm not surprised at all to know that the OSCE established some sort of body to honour developments in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both Germany and the OSCE called this the Crisis Staff. Do you know that Croatia had a Crisis Staff at the level of Croatia and in each and every municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There just seemed to be Crisis Staffs everywhere, and in -- in former Yugoslavia. I don't accept -- I don't accept -- I'd want to see that Germany and the OSCE used the word "Crisis Staff," for their -- their body -- their bodies, but I'm not surprised to find -- would I not be surprised to find that Crisis Staffs existed at the level of one or more governmental bodies or -- at individual municipalities in Croatia. I don't -- I very much doubt that there was a Crisis Staff at every -- in every municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see whether that's how it was. Do you know that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina established the Crisis Staff also in September of 1991 and that Ejup Ganic was in charge of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I actually reported on that in my submission, one of the three papers that I prepared for this -- this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I read out a very brief passage from the middle column about what Professor Plavsic said as the chairman of the council for preservation of constitutional order. She says: "When I was appointed to the Crisis Staff, whose president is Dr. Ejup Ganic, I believed that some urgent matters would be resolved such as, for example, accommodation for refugees, ensuring food and the similar. However, the Crisis Staff started getting involved in affairs which are far from its area of responsibilities. By expanding on what this was about, Dr. Biljana Plavsic pointed out that the Crisis Staff took over the responsibilities of the council for All People's Defence." And then further down Biljana says: "Can you believe it? The situation is what it is, and the council for All People's Defence is not functioning, whereas the Crisis Staff took everything upon itself." And then further down it says that she concluded that an informal group was actually allowed to deal with the most delicate problems. So, Professor Plavsic and Professor Koljevic at the time publicly stated that Ejup Ganic was establishing the Crisis Staff in order to circumvent the Serbs in the Presidency and in order to do things that actually do not belong within the remit of the Crisis Staff. Was there a single Serbian Crisis Staff in existence on the 20th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence. Can it be marked for identification and translated, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On this one, Your Honour, I do object. The entire article is not displayed. Dr. Karadzic has only read out one small passage of the article. We have no translation from which to be able to assess the context and other statements of the article, and frankly, Your Honour, the question that was asked of Dr. Donia had absolutely nothing to do with the passage of the article that Dr. Karadzic read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct. You may call Professor Plavsic if necessary. We will not admit this. Dr. Donia didn't confirm anything about this. This is just a news clipping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Donia confirmed that he had written about Crisis Staffs, and this is an article about Crisis Staffs and a member of the Presidency, Dr. Biljana Plavsic. So please reconsider. This is a document that speaks of the same matter. I asked Dr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia testified he knew about the Crisis Staff of the BiH, and he knew that Mr. Ganic was appointed as chairman. That's the farthest he can testify, but he has nothing to do with Plavsic's comment. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you know that Mrs. Plavsic resigned because she considered that that was an informal group that was doing things that it wasn't supposed to do things that it was doing? She resigned from her position in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that plausible, but I don't know when she resigned. If -- I mean, if -- she continued to actively head up this council for constitutional preservation, or whatever it was, for many more months after this. What -- I can certainly affirm that, but what she did with the Crisis Staff, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, she resigned on the 3rd of October. Do you remember that this staff was disbanded pursuant to a request of the -- on the 2nd or 3rd March after the people were killed at the barricades? It was disbanded at the request of one of the political parties. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your question was not translated in full, I gather. Pursuant to a request of what?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to the request of the Serbian Democratic Party. After the barricades -- or, rather, while the barricades were there a session was held to which Mr. Lukic was invited. He set out his requests, and one of the requests was to disband this illegal body, this Crisis Staff, whereas Professor Plavsic resigned on the 3rd of October, claiming that it was an illegal body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's two different time frames you're speaking of here, I think. And as to the one on the 2nd, 3rd of March at the time of the barricades, the SDS had established its own Crisis Staff at that time which was headed by Mr. Dukic, because at that time you were in Belgrade, as I recall, and it wasn't clear to me whether Mrs. Plavsic was a member of that Crisis Staff or not. That was, I think, one of those Crisis Staffs that lasted about something like 48 hours and then disbanded. Now, at that time, if there was an initiative to disband the Crisis Staff, it would have been of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'm not aware of that. I don't see the Crisis Staff of the Presidency doing very much at that time, but perhaps I'm just not seeing any -- seeing activity that -- that may have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Chamber reconsider or consider the admission into evidence of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the answer is simply no. Evidence is Dr. Donia's response to your questions. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have 65 ter 11311.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, now we are coming to the key point in your testimony, and I also believe to the key point of the indictment, which is the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, when an Assembly session was held at which the memorandum on sovereignty was adopted. We need page 1 to 2 in Serbian, and in English page 116. Did you see the entire minutes from this Assembly session, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read them, yes. Not recently, but I've read through them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you read in the entirety everything that I said on that day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that this speech is of huge importance for the indictment and that now we should deal with this speech as a central development and that session as the also central point for the indictment. I don't know whether the OTP has the audio recording of that session. It would be good if they did. If not, I will just read certain passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer that question, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not immediately Your Honour, but I'm just wondering why Dr. Karadzic would need to read certain passages when we have a full translation of the transcript in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could have asked that question earlier. Let's move on with this transcript, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I will have to read out certain passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Before explaining the proposal, whether I will do it or somebody else, I have to explain something which stems from the interpretation of what we say at this speakers' platform. That thing is namely related to the issue of war and peace. For the hundredth time I have to repeat that the Serbs do not threaten with war. Serbs only make it public that they would not be able to accept any decision reached by out-voting and to their detriment and that the Serbs could not be forced to live in the state that they do not want. Serbs and Muslims, we understand each other well. That is, Muslims are afraid that they will become a minority in the -- in the Rump Yugoslavia, even though they enjoy the protection of the republic which would never become a constituent part of Serbia but which would be completely equal to Serbia. So Serbs are also afraid that in Bosnia-Herzegovina they would be out-voted now or several years later. It is completely the same. Please, gentlemen, Muslim leaders have clearly stated so far that should this catastrophe occur, it would, above all, be the catastrophe of Muslim people and also the catastrophe for the Serbs and Croats as well, especially the Serbs and Muslims since we are mixed in Serbia. While Serbs and Croats in Serbia are pretty distant from the geographical point of view except in the big cities, naturally." Now, did you have this part of the speech in mind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "in mind"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take into consideration the entirety of this speech when you produced your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg for your patience, but everybody can, of course, read for themselves. We can skip over some parts and then I will -- it reads that the Serbs had never attacked Muslims, nor would they ever attack Muslims, nor is there such a sentiment among the Serbs in relation to Muslims. In the English it's on the following page. But the chaos that could be produced by the illegal out-voting, the chaos that could be produced, the chaos that nobody would start, but the chaos that has it's own logic, the one that we spoke about here, somebody has control over the order. The chaos is not in -- is in nobody's hands. Nobody has control over it. The basic characteristic of chaos is that nobody generates it. Rather, it has its own logic and generates itself. This is why in such a chaos there could be wrong intentions above all, intentions of the Muslim leadership to perhaps do something that would be good for the Muslims but would not be good for the Serbs. This could produce a chaos which would be beyond anybody's control. But to make it clear, the Serb Democratic Party does not support chaos, and precisely because we do not support chaos, we keep insisting that not a single decision be passed that would be against any nation in Yugoslavia or any nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know for sure that should there be chaos, Serbs, Muslims and Croats would suffer, especially Serbs and Muslims, just as today a mine or grenade does not choose whose house it will hit in Croatia or Slavonia. This is page 117 in the English. Did you take into consideration, did you comment on this position of mine in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my report I characterised this as an impassioned speech, and I think I hear that same passion as you read it again today, and there is no doubt in my mind that when you said it then or you read it now that you really believe this. I look at it as a very aggressive statement of the position that you've taken on -- you had taken on out-voting, that is, the right to veto any -- any measure at the same time that you were incorporating repeated protestations of innocence and peaceful intentions. And as I say, I don't have any reason to doubt any of that. I think I probably didn't capture fully the entire argument that you're presenting here, but I believe that in referencing the speech and the paper on formation of Republika Srpska I, in fact, did take note of what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get to the aggression a bit later. Let's see a few sentences down there: "This is how we can announce that there would be no war, that there would be no chaos, because we control the order, and chaos is in nobody's hands any longer." In English it begins with the words, "I ask you." "I ask you to think about this and to say --" this is seven lines from the bottom, seven lines up. So our position is that we control the order and nobody controls chaos, and you think that this was an impassioned speech supporting the war; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I called it an impassioned speech in total, some of it impassioned very much in protesting the desire not to have war. I characterised the entire speech as impassioned. I think you got very animated -- I guess you're not interested in my answer because you're not listening to it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm listening to you. Sure, continue, but, Mr. Donia, you wish to say that this is a war mongering speech. Thank you very much. Let me continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness complete his answer, please. Dr. Donia, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I characterised the entire speech as impassioned, and I believe you became more animated and more -- louder and more impassioned as the speech went along, right up until the last few lines. So as I say, I don't have any reason to doubt the sincerity of your -- your words here, that you felt very strongly about it and presented varying points of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Donia -- here. Would you say it was a war mongering speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 106 in the English version of this document. Let's skip over as much material as we can, but the Chamber has the entire minutes at its disposal, as does the OTP. See here, it says: "Gentlemen." I did not appear here as the God of war as somebody described me. Can you lower this down. Page 106, lower please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Last -- last paragraph, bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do not appear here as the God of war, which is how somebody from the Croatian Democratic Party depicted me. I repeated for the hundredth time, and I said it in our conversations, "It is not the Serbian Democratic Party that creates the will of the Serbian people, rather it interprets it." Did you take this into consideration, namely that the Serbian people exist, that the nation has its own will and that no party can impose its opinion on the nation, rather, a political party serves the nation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is what I have been referring to. I think you absolutise the notion of the Serbian people, make it into an anthropomorphic concept and reduce its will to whatever the Serbian Democratic Party determines it to be, and you, yourself, determine what the position of the SDP is. I think you've personalised, in that sense, a will of a group that you postulate as existing and just ran with that -- that belief from well before this and express it very clearly here. I think your -- your words are absolutely clear on what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that we invented it or we heard this from the people? Do you know that we organised referendums?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point you hadn't yet organised a referendum, I believe. You had the election, of course, but I don't believe at this point there had been a referendum yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You agreed that there were 86 Serbs at the parliament out of this and 82 in the Serbian Democratic Party. Do you remember that out of those 86, 83 Serb members of the parliament supported this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we talked about this election results before and just to point out that -- that the voting that took place for the Presidency, the two SDS candidates out of the four top Serb vote-getters, the SDS candidates received 58 per cent of the votes, and I think it was about 558.000 for Mr. Koljevic, 570.000 votes for Mrs. Plavsic. Mr. Kecmanovic got 500.000 votes. He was not a member of the SDS. Mr. Pejanovic, I think, got about 350.000 votes. So I grant your point about the number of delegates in the -- in the parliament, in the Assembly, but that does not derive from a high percentage that is the numbers that you've suggested, 90 or more plus per cent of the actual votes that were delivered for candidates of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Donia, we had less than 32 per cent in the general population, and we won 31 per cent of the votes. This is what I keep insisting on. But let us stick to what you said. I'm not discussing the Presidency. Kecmanovic and other delegates also supported our platform, and this involves all Serbian delegates but three, which is to say that only 4 or 5 per cent of Serbian delegates did not take part of this. Out of 86 the three didn't, but all other 83 did, and they did not represent only the Serbian Democratic Party. Is that how it was, that there were 83 delegates back then and also today in the Serbian parliament?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see English page 108. This is still my speech which is essential for everything we're dealing with now, so that's why I ask you to be patient. I say here: "We do not object you starting the initiative for amending the constitution." It's page 106. It should be the page before. It may be even page 105. At the bottom of 105. No, no, 107. I apologise: "We do not care if you submit ..." "We do not object --" it's not translated well: "We do not object, we do not oppose you submitting an initiative to amend the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it will not work that way. It has to pass through the constitutional commission and then to the chamber of citizens and a vote should be taken there, but, again, you cannot interfere in the matters that are regulated by the federal constitution. I am trying in the most peaceful way to tell you this as well. The Serbian people know what you want. You want to achieve -- to ensure in The Hague that this would become the third or the fourth republic that does not wish to exist in Yugoslavia, and that is not true, because we want to live in Yugoslavia. You can speak for yourselves. All sovereign people in Bosnia-Herzegovina should speak for themselves. No other group of people should do it on their behalf. We even reached such a conclusion at this Assembly. We will prevent you before domestic and international public from -- from implementing violence against the Serbian people, the constitutional violence, because after constitutional violence all other types of violence could follow. "This has been repeated here hundred of times. We do not have any say in the situation if we get into the situations in which Slovenia and Croatia are, especially because this hell in Bosnia and Herzegovina would be thousand times more grave, and there would be no way to stop it." And then further down: "I ask you, once again, I'm not threatening, I'm asking you to take seriously the interpretation of the political will of the Serbian people ..." A better interpretation would have been, "I beg you. I'm begging you." And then further down: "I'm pleading with you to take this seriously, that this is not the proper way, that the road that you chose for Bosnia and Herzegovina is the same highway of hell and suffering which Slovenia and Croatia had taken. Do not think that you will not take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell, and Muslim people into obliteration, because should there and a war, Muslim people would not be able to defend themselves." And then somebody said that these were big words, and then I said: "Well, big situations require big words. How will you prevent people from killing each other in Bosnia and Herzegovina?" Do you still claim that this is a war mongering speech, a belligerent speech?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated in answer to -- to Your Honour's question, I believe that the very last part of it is, and essentially the last six or seven sentences that you have read in the context of the time, with their repeated references to violence and parallel republics in which wars had raged or were raging and the manner of your delivery made this into what I would call a -- a brief but final part -- or brief warmongering part of an overall speech that otherwise was not. And I would have to share the rather understated response of Mr. Izetbegovic, who asked for the floor just after you finished, in which he said that the message you delivered and the manner in which you delivered it gave good reason to doubt whether we can, that is he was speaking of Bosnia, can remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the previous session of the Assembly Muhamed Filipovic had uttered the same words: "If things go this way, my people will disappear"? Did you notice that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not -- I've not seen that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is quite literally the previous session of the Assembly. However, now let's go back to the beginning. The beginning is actually the end of the speech, when we said we have to clarify things. 116 in English. We have to clarify a particular matter that stems from the interpretation of what we're saying from this rostrum. This actually has to do with an issue of war and peace. We have to repeat for the hundredth time that the Serbs are not threatening with war. They are simply making it public that they will not be able to accept any decision that is reached by out-voting. Mr. Donia, do you believe that I was supposed to deceive the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to say to them, Just go ahead, the Serbs will accept that, when I know full well that the Serbs would not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you were clearly speaking on behalf here of the SDS and what you envisioned as the Serb people, and you were speaking to a member -- or to a body of which you were not a member. So clearly you were there in your capacity as president of the party, and I think you were delivering the message on behalf of the party and certainly what you believed to be the near unanimous opinion of the Serb people. So I don't believe you were trying to deceive anybody with these pronouncements. I think you were speaking out of genuine conviction and of representing your view points very forcefully, even angrily, but straightforwardly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see, Mr. Donia, even if the Serb Democratic Party had had 51 per cent of the support of the Serb people, they are a legitimate representative. However, I am speaking here because I have the support of 83 MPs out of a total of 86 Serbs -- Serb MPs. That is more than two-thirds from the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than two-thirds of the what? Of the Serb --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: More than one-third of the total number of MPs. There is a total number of 248 [as interpreted] MPs, and I have the support of over 80 MPs. Eighty is one-third; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point on this -- I think on this issue you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 240. The transcript says 248. So can this be corrected. And I'm not talking about the Serb Democratic Party anywhere over here. I'm talking about Serb people because I have the support of 83 MPs. Ten days before that they had separated into the Serb Assembly. Thank you. Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The -- about three minutes of the audio of this speech is in evidence. The whole audio of this speech is found at 65 ter 45005.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and it's also transcribed. If we are limiting matters to this speech itself, I actually understood Dr. Karadzic earlier on to be talking about the audio file of the whole session, which was what we are trying to fine, and my apologies for my misunderstanding. In any case, the three minutes is -- has -- which is the portion that we played in Dr. Donia's examination-in-chief is -- has been admitted as P959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That contains only the last part of his minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 45005 contains whole speech of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, but to be a hundred per cent sure, I should have somebody check that so that we -- just to confirm that we don't have anything missing at one end or the other, and I could probably have that done in fairly short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that Mr. Karadzic wanted to show us the video-tape, we are minded to admit all the video-clip as well as the transcript. So what is the practice? We admit it in separately or altogether? I'll consult the Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So video-tape together with the transcript will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify, that will be 65 ter 45005. That will be Exhibit D267.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the English translation, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic. With the assistance of the OTP, you should tender the CD that contains that relevant video to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope that I will receive that, because I think that what I receive from the OTP was only this part that could be used against me, whereas I would like the Trial Chamber to see the speech in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, no, Your Honour. The 65 ter 45005 was disclosed in 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe some problem in locating it, so in that case I have no doubt that Ms. Edgerton would be so kind to assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, this is the 14th and 15th of October; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This comes after everything we had been through before the elections, and then there were the elections and then the division of power and then the first months of government, the attempt to reach a historic agreement between the Serbs and Muslims, the 11th of September, the agreement on not imposing a solution and the legitimacy of all options, and then on the 14th and 15th we have this out-voting. Do you think that it is possible to pass constitutional decisions in an unconstitutional way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm just completely baffled myself about what the constitution said -- says about this, about the action that was -- that was subsequently taken. I have always thought it looked to me more like a matter of the rules of order of the Assembly than the constitution, but I really don't -- don't know if that's the case and wouldn't pretend to -- to interpret it. I can certainly tell you that you viewed it as unconstitutional and illegal and had for some time before that. That was very clear. And others either didn't comment on it or believed it to be in accord with the constitution. Big controversy about it, but whether it was against the constitution or not, I can't make that judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now have 1230. Do you have -- do you know the name Rasim Kadic [Realtime transcript read in error "Tadic"]?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- I believe I have the right Kadic here. I think it's wrong in the transcript. It's Kadic. Was the president of the -- was it delegates club of the SDA, I believe. He was in the Assembly and spoke for the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Naim Kadic. Yes, you have a good memory, don't you. But this is Rasim Kadic. He is also a Muslim, but he is the president of a liberal party, right, that came into being on the basis of what used to be the youth party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that this is not what we asked for. 1290, 1290 is what we're asking for, that is the conversation between myself and Mr. Rasim Kadic on the 16th of October, and in this conversation Rasim Kadic informs me that he had not voted and that his party had not voted in favour of this memorandum on sovereignty, and he said that the road was now open for extra institutional behaviour. I believe that the OTP has a translation. Yes. Yes, here it is. The first page is not really very important. Could we have the next page, please. Could I have the next page in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Rasim Kadic, the third line: "I feel it is necessary after everything that had happened for us to meet on a party basis during the course of the next few days, if you can accept that," and then I say, "Well, yes, we can agree on that." And then Rasim Kadic says: "Radovan Karadzic, I am convinced that you know that all of this is illegal and that it has nothing to do with anything whatsoever. The shame that I am now -- is the disgrace that I announced from the stand, that is something that nobody in Europe will be able to swallow." Rasim Kadic says: "I have to say that I didn't take part in the vote, nor do I want to." And I ask: "You did not participate in the vote, did you?" And Rasim Kadic says: "Of course not. Read today's newspapers." And so on and so forth: "I want you to clear things up in government." And then I say: "Well, we kept saying other things for three months. Mr. Izetbegovic and I had almost reached an agreement and to finish the job so that the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina could breathe an sigh of relief. Everybody would have had their own part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not split by pickets but in an institutional sense as it used to be it Turkish times. It's all known Taslihan is over here." You know what Taslihan is? That is the part of Sarajevo where the Serbs used to live in Turkish times. Mr. Donia, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Turkish district is over here and Latinluk is over there. That's where the Catholic used to live. Everyone minds their own business and all of them together deal with what is everybody's business. That would be possible to do as well. Some would have been involved in Yugoslavia a little but would have been involved more as they pleased. We would have found that it was unique solution, Europe, similar to the one that existed in Switzerland, but not that one. However, all of a sudden all these talks -- after all these talks a paper showed up which was completely different, that is a disgrace, and so on and so forth. Now Rasim Kadic says -- can we move on to the next page so that I don't read everything out. The next page please. The next page. Now, Mr. Rasim Kadic says he doesn't want to mediate. He is trying to find a possibility to -- that would leave to an alleviation of the situation and then he says -- I have to find that part now. He said that in that way the road was open -- yes, here it is the third one, yes, but it is obvious that the mistakes of others are giving rise to an extra institutional solution to the crisis, so that suits no one. This is a Muslim, the president of the Liberal Party. He did not vote, and he is calling me the very next day with sympathy and support, and he is seeking a solution, and he says that the road had been opened for extra institutional behaviour. Were you aware of that? Have you seen this intercept before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence, this intercept? For identification, MFI, because it's an intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 6416. Could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, this was the pinnacle of an intensive political life that had started once political parties were established, when multi-party democracy was introduced. Now I would like us to have a look at something. I'm afraid it's not this. 14 -- no, 6416. 6416. That's the 65 ter number. Now I would like to deal with this as briefly as possible and to see what the state of mind of Radovan Karadzic was in July 1990. Let us see what it was that he was thinking, feeling, and saying, Radovan Karadzic, and what it was that he advocated from then up until this moment, that is to say the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before reading out something, you could -- should tell the witness, as well as to the Chamber, what this document is about. You said pinnacle. What is pinnacle?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pinnacle of the crisis, Your Excellency, is the 15th of October, when there was a collapse in all our talks and when there was the walkout of the Serb MPs and when the Assembly was established, when the chances of resolving things differently went down the drain. Temporarily though. However, up until the end of March we tried. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether it was your interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Mistake. 6146. 6146. This is my interview from the 20th of July, 1990. My intention is to see mens rea in this way, to see what the state of mind of Radovan Karadzic was from that moment onwards until the 15th of October, and I believe that Mr. Donia is quite familiar with this. He has already spoken about it. Actually, during the first day of cross-examination he made a reference to it. The interview is available to all in it's entirety. I think that the OTP got it, but would I like to call up page 10 in English. Answer number 68.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What publication is this in, sir? I'm afraid I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let's go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Nin." That was the most eminent news magazine in all of Yugoslavia at that time. It was a weekly news magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, are you satisfied with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Then let's go back to that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sixty-eight or 67. The journalist is saying, Are you talking about reconciliation? Karadzic says, Reconciliation is indispensable. The Serbs need to seek peace with others and to forgive as much as possible. We shouldn't be forcing anyone to repent. The penitent himself has to have motivation and moral strength, otherwise there is no use. The Serbs also have to reconcile themselves amongst themselves. The civil war amongst the Serb people has to be brought to an end because it has already brought so much evil. You see I'm talking about the clash between the Royalists and the Republicans, that is to say the Communists. I'm talking about the inter-Serb conflict or clash; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Partisan Chetnik, is that what you're suggesting? Partisan-Chetnik clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The first part has to do with our reconciliation with other peoples; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move on to 69. However, reconciliation does not mean that the vanquished should rise to the position of victor by dragging the victors down to the place where the defeating were kept in the past. That would also mean a continuation of the civil war. Both the victors and the defeated must leave their positions, their trenches, and meet each other halfway. Do you remember that I had asked for Serbs to stop being both Serbs and Chetniks, rather, to be a modern European people without any such divisions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was you in July 1990, was frankly the Radovan Karadzic that I liked, who was expressing, I think, a very realistic and sober assessment of the situation amongst the political parties and the assessment of the needs of Serbs to put behind them these clashes from the past between Chetniks and partisans. I mean, it's not my testimony or my account that would paint you as having, back at this time, the kind of animosities that you displayed nor the kind of hard-line positions that you assumed later on in the conflict. I think -- you know, I agreed with you from going back to your days living with and amongst Muslims and your working with Meho as your barber and other things, about that period of your life. I have no problem agreeing with what you actually state here and acknowledging it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that we'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence, this interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D269, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tieger, your motion regarding the witness who is supposed to come at the end of the month, my understanding is that you asked for a leave to reply to the response of the accused, which is now granted, but I wonder whether you can do it by today, end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. If there's any reason to think otherwise, we'll let the Court know immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's granted. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have 65 ter 31805 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And to to inform you, Mr. Donia, about what I'm going to put to you now, there's a number of these interviews, and you probably saw most of them, and they go along these lines all the way up until February of 1991, and at some future occasion I will tender them into evidence, but I would like now to shed light on the issue of war and peace when it comes to political developments. This is an intercept of a conversation between me and Vitomir Zepinic. It is very interesting, and we will go back to it regarding other issues, because here you can see that I didn't know him. I didn't know Mandic or anybody else, but we will get back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 13 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at -- I guess the interpreters would need the Serbian version, and for you it is this portion here: "Tomorrow is the question ..." "Tomorrow is the issue of the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a little bit. The interpreters wanted to see the B/C/S version. In the meantime, Doctor, do you know who Mr. Zepinic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Both of them on the screen --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the beginning. Both versions are in B/C/S. One can be in English. It's okay. Let me just tell the others that Vitomir Zepinic was the highest Serbian representative in the Ministry of the Interior. Muslims were given the office of the minister, and the Serbs were allocated the position of the deputy minister, and Zepinic was nominated for that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, do you agree with his --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just noting that that was in accord with the inter-party agreements that were reached in the formation of the government in January 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, however since in your presentation, your comment does not constitute evidence. Evidence should come through the witness's words. Let's move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm rushing. I wish to inform you as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The words where it begins, "Tomorrow is the question," so I say to Zepinic: "Tomorrow is the question of the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have no chance or anyway of changing anything there. Either -- neither the people nor the deputies would accept any exception. Bosnian will remain in Yugoslavia until some of its peoples decide differently. And this will be clearly seen tomorrow. Tomorrow, maybe the political system -- or, rather, maybe Bosnia-Herzegovina would collapse and then it would be the end, but we can't help there. We cannot bow our heads down. There's no way we can do that. We're absolutely determined and absolutely clean in that sense." And then his following comments goes. And Karadzic says again: "No. We don't stand a change. Well, I can say -- I can go in front of the Assembly and say that we accept sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina and then --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the interpreters are following very -- in an excellent manner, but the e-court does not show the relevant B/C/S page, I gather.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S it should be page 9, I think. Page 9 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So then I say: "In two hours there will be chaos in Bosnia." And then I say, "Even were I to accept it, nothing would come out of it because chaos would ensue in two hours." And then could we see the next page in the English version. Then I say: "I have neither right, no efficiency, because in two hours there would be chaos in Bosnia-Herzegovina." So I inform the deputy minister here that even were I to accept, were I to say that we accept the sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there would be chaos on the ground and there would be no control over the process. Have you seen this intercept?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted in the way that intercepts are admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D270, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is still the month of June of 1991. Could we now have 65 ter 30055, which is an intercept with Mr. Vukic, a physician from Banja Luka, who was the regional head of the SDS. In English we need page 2, and in Serbian page 3, please. We will now only deal with the issue of war and peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I rarely intervene, but as regards the previous intercept, having read out all the parts, your only question to the witness was whether he has seen that intercept. What's the point of reading out all the contents of the document? Bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that Mr. Donia produced his report on the basis of everything he had seen, and I'm interested in learning whether he had seen this. If he did see it, then we also have to see how this affected his expert report, and I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: See here, in page 2 in English, I inform Mr. Vukic, and I say: "I think that it is clear now that Izetbegovic wants to wage war." And then he mentions Babic, and then I say he is basically doing things that favour the belligerent Izetbegovic. Do you remember that I always had to fight against Babic's actions in Bosanska Krajina which favoured the split of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I think you've mentioned this; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite right. I think you at times brought him into play in support of your initiatives; and at other times, in fact, most of the time, both you and Mr. Milosevic found him to be a royal pain who kept messing up your plans, and I think what you keep referring to here is the looming initiative of both the Serbs of -- the Serbs of both the Bosnian Krajina and the Krajina in Croatia to proclaim unity, the unity of the two Krajinas which was something they were planning to do toward the end of June. So it stands to make sense to me here that you were speaking with Mr. Vukic in an effort to -- the beginning of your effort to head off this impending union. You followed that up with some other efforts to do it, and eventually when it was proclaimed sort of let it die of neglect. But the -- the role of Babic in that was he was clearly a provocateur and he was promoting it by his travels to Banja Luka as part of officially representing the -- the Krajina in Croatia and linking up with some of your own people, SDS leaders, in Banja Luka in preparation for proclaiming this union which was -- would have been a real, I think, something the international community would have found extremely distasteful and dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can it be gleaned on the basis of this that I was against the war and that I believed that Izetbegovic wanted to wage a war and that Babic's provocations could give justification to Izetbegovic for his actions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in some sense these are very general anodyne statements that do, in fact, correspond with your position on what Babic was about to do, but I -- I wouldn't accept the -- the premise that they in general refer to -- or that reflect your belief that Izetbegovic wants a war and so does Babic. I wouldn't go that far. I think in the context in which you are speaking with Mr. Vukic here, they refer to this specific issue of the union of two Krajinas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted, this intercept? I will be going back to this intercept when dealing with other topics too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D271, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 31813.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is my intercept. We're still in June. 24th of June, 1991. It is a conversation between Karadzic, Zepinic, and Mandic. Momcilo Mandic is also one of the officials of the Ministry of the Interior and he was a Serbian candidate; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see page 2 in English and also page 2 in Serbian. I'm having a conversation with Zepinic here, and I say that I went to Nevesinje and that some Muslim paramilitaries had beaten up three young men. There were some 20 of them. They beat three young men, and they were armed with this particular kind of weapon. And then I go on to say that I told them that they shouldn't do anything unlawful there at any cost, even if they are beaten, even if they have great suffering. And then four lines down I say because I know what is behind it. And then I go on to say there is a need to provoke, and Zepinic says chaos and provocation, and I say provocation and only when Serbs are in majority. So precisely in places where Serbs are in majority will let it develop into, and so on. And then I mention Visegrad and then I say and this thing with Visegrad is a disgrace. It will put pressure on Izetbegovic. This is page 2 in English still. And I go on to say that an Orthodox priest in Visegrad was pulled by his beard, and then we go on to say that in Visegrad the Muslim side had already put up a border toward Serbia. Have you seen this intercept before during your preparations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see it prior to preparing my report. I have seen it since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can it be seen on the basis of then that I pleaded with them, saying that they should suffer, put up with all the sufferings and that they should let -- they should put up with beatings even just in order to preserve peace?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again I think based on the context here I would attribute a more limited significance to your comments, to the statements that you made here. This was taking place at a time that there was indeed a general unrest taking place, much of it under the agitation of Mr. Vucurevic in Eastern Herzegovina. That entailed rallies, some Serb nationalist rhetoric, and a -- enough of a threatening situation so that some Muslim representatives from that area made a trip to the Presidency in Sarajevo and expressed concern about being forced to emigrate from that area at this time. And I -- I take it that this is part of your effort to reassure the two people who would have a lot to say about it that the party was, you know, the party was, in fact, wanted to calm things down, that the party was well-intentioned toward the issue of war and peace in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, so far you have tendered the intercepts in several occasions as evidence, so at this point of time can I get a sort of clarification from you what your attitude as to the intercept is. My understanding is that you are generally opposed to the admission of intercepts into evidence. So is it your position that only those you are referring to should be admitted into evidence or that you are not objecting to the admission of them into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, for me these intercepts are first and foremost an evidence showing that the Muslim authorities intercepted in an unlawful way conversations of Serbian authorities. Why unlawful? Because this could not be done without the decision of the court and approval of the Presidency, and those are lacking. And the main prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Serb. He was not a member of the SDS but was nominated by the SDS. So this just serves as evidence that they were intercepting our conversations, that they were unloyal partners. So this is my general objection. And I don't know whether you will admit this or not. I'm doing this just wanting to show what it is that I uttered in my telephone conversations without knowing that this would be intercepted or presented as evidence. If, however, none of this is every going to be admitted, then it's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll leave it there, and then let's continue. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D272, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 65 ter 07288.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have probably seen this. These are shorthand minutes from the Assembly of the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 12th of June, 1991, St. Peter's and Paul's day, just so that you know what it is about. So English page 133. You know, that this was the first Assembly held after the SDS had been in existence for one year and then -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see that the fight, which is the next page in the Serbian, 118, and I'm talking to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 118 in the Serbian version, please. Another two pages. 118, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here you see that the -- "this fight has been taking place in the parliament. It's good that it is taking place in the parliament rather than in the streets. We will do nothing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. B/C/S page should show the 118. Yes, that's correct. The bottom part. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a feeling that you speak Serbian, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you see that: "This fight has been taking place in the parliament. It is good that it is taking place in the parliament rather than in the streets. We will do nothing to contribute to this fight spilling into the streets." And then I continue saying: "This is why we have no need for that or anything else except for the strengthening of the JNA which is unfortunately the only federal constitution that we can have trust in." So do you see that back on the 12th of July, 1991, we had a very firm position against the street fights?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think this is a very -- it's a lengthy speech by you and followed by some by others that contains a lot of different viewpoints on -- on major issues, and -- I mean, one of them that is clearly interesting here is how you've basically rejected the federal institutions except for the Yugoslav People's Army, which raises the question of the significance one would attach to your two previous sentences. So I would -- and then repeat your subsequent remarks here about Mr. Markovic and Mr. Mesic who were the representatives of the federal Prime Minister and the president of the Presidency, respectively. So it isn't here clear here which parliament you're speaking of. Was it the parliament of federal Yugoslavia? Was it the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina? It's -- it's certainly a statement of your desire to keep conflicts within parliamentary boundaries, but it's also, I think, a nuance somewhat by some of the remarks that you make surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm referring to the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You have sensed this well. We will go back to the JNA. All I'm doing now is showing that, and this is something that you identified yourself, what we wanted was to keep the fighting in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it hasn't been admitted yet, we will admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 31843, please. Unfortunately, we do not have the translation here, but I will read this out. It is quite brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There should and translation available and uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much again. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. This is my conversation with Dragan Djokanovic, a physician on the 26th of July, and he was the chairman of the Democratic Party of Federalists. It was a small party which was not represented in the parliament but was quite active in preserving the federation. Do you remember Dragan Djokanovic? Have you seen that name before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall what -- what his position was or what party he belonged to, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Democratic Party of Federalists?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of it. I don't really know what its programme was or anything more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here I say: "Because Alija --" this is the last sentence in the English, I say: "Because Alija has nowhere to go. It's a dead end. All the legal matters are in our hands, and if they were to do something stupid to us now, because the Muslims are turning fiercely against Alija's war-bent intentions." And then on the English side -- on the English page, next page in English, and then I say: "The Muslims who are opposed to the war." It's the next page in English: "The Muslims who do not want to wage war. They have a republic. They have Yugoslavia. No sane person wants to wage war, and Alija wants to wage war in order to change it. Now Alija cannot explain to the Muslim people were they should wage war, and if they do something stupid, then he could say to them, well, this is why you should wage war." So here I explain to Mr. Djokanovic, who is a chairman of a small political party why I was against some minor stupid things that our people did, saying that that would play into the hands of Alija's wish to wage war. And then in the Serbian text we need the next page. I go there to say that now he needs an alibi -- alibi for the war, and we should not aid him in this. So do you remember that at this time, on the 26th of July, the preparations for the historic agreement that we had with Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic was quite advanced and that these were the Muslims that I was referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that adds the proper context to this -- this conversation. It was at that time when the -- again I think of it as the Belgrade initiative, or, if you want to, the grand agreement or historical agreement between the Serbs and Muslims. This efforts was underway and both you and Milosevic had decided that the best way to pursue it was to undermine Izetbegovic and force him or somehow influence him to make this agreement come about. It was then your -- it was mainly Milosevic's idea to hold a series of meetings or rallies in Bosnia, the first of which I think was held about the -- I don't know, the 8th or 10th of July, and then this one obviously planned for the 2nd of August. And these were represented as peace rallies. The one that isn't clear to me exactly where this one was scheduled for. The one I'm more familiar with was in Sarajevo, and so in pursuit of this agreement, which I agree the -- you and Milosevic desperately wanted to get this agreement to get Bosnia, all of Bosnia, to remain a part of Yugoslavia as the other republics broke away, that this was part of that effort to represent the ambitions of the party at this point as purely peaceful and as allied against any anybody who was pursuing war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Leaving Milosevic aside, who had joined in and Izetbegovic who had approved, but do you agree that the honour of the initiators of the agreement should go to Zulfikarpasic? Right? Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Professor Filipovic were the initiators of this proposal. They walked into your office, as I understand it, and proposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you do remember that they had said that Professor Koljevic and I joyfully accepted that. That is what Filipovic wrote in his book; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I don't doubt it a bit. I mean, I the -- these two people who were also the principles of a minor party that got no traction, really, in the elections, were at that time doing all sorts of things to try to gain support or take support away from the SDA and to criticise and, in a sense, marginalise Izetbegovic, and even though they co-operated with him well in some areas, this was very much a part of their effort to get some traction and attention to their party, and they did, indeed, avidly pursue this arrangement with you and Mr. Milosevic when they went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, do you agree that the agreement was reached in Sarajevo and that work was done on it, but Belgrade joined in eventually because Zulfikarpasic wanted a broader framework? Yes or no? Were the main protagonists of the agreement in Sarajevo the SDS and the MBO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my understanding of -- of it at that point. I -- I think that when the -- when the idea first came about and they walked into your office and you met, I think at the SDS headquarters, you walked into the next room, called Milosevic and arranged for them to go -- or for at least Zulfikarpasic to go up there the next day, and they had a conversation that next day in which he offered a number of things in order to secure the agreement and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
