utterances.text: And if -- you know, I really -- I'm trying to answer your questions. I'm trying to listen carefully to what you ask me and hope that you listen to what I have to say to you. Subsequently, Milosevic and you were in touch, but he actually then sort of delegated to you and actors in Bosnia the primary responsibility for reaching the agreement, drafting it, and then he reviewed its terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I'm listening to what you're saying, and I'm reading this, so I see exactly what your answer is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this intercept be admitted into evidence just like all the rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D274, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 31849 is the 65 ter number I'd like now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is already the 1st of August. Before I deal with this, I'd like to ask you whether you remember that Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic confirmed that we went to see Izetbegovic together and that he asked that we go on with the agreement and that he actually said that he had lost the confidence of the Serbs and that it's better for the MBO to pursue this.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's generally my -- in general my understanding. Maybe not the specific words, but that was the -- the essence of the agreement that you reached at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have page 4 in English. Page 4 in English, and in Serbian it's also 4. It's the 1st of August, and I am saying -- I'm speaking to Mr. Krajisnik, actually. He is asking me whether I attended that commission, that conference, and I said yes. I said that we had disclosed that and that it is prepared for signing, and once the peoples get their bearings and reach agreement, then -- and he says: "Alija says that?" Yes. I said I did not talk to him about that. And then I say here, "Politika" carried the news that he would -- that he said that they would fight if there's a war. The Muslim would fight on the side of the Croats. And Krajisnik says a-ha, and I say I thinking it something really terrible and then further down, now we have to tell the Muslims whether what Alija is saying is correct. Do you see that? In the midst of our talks Izetbegovic made a statement saying that the Muslims would fight on the side of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm following this correctly, that was something published in "Politika," and I would, on that basis, raise serious questions about its reliability, because while "Nin" was indeed a quality publication at that time, "Politika" had become basically a voice, a mouthpiece for the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, there's no doubt that I did read that and that I was making comments when speaking to Krajisnik that this was terrible and that we will have to see whether what Alija is saying is correct. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D275, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 30136, 65 ter. 30136, 65 ter. Again, Karadzic/Krajisnik, on the 7th of August. As for the other aspects, we'll deal with them on some other occasion. Now we are just going to deal with the issues of war and peace. So it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see the date. We're waiting for the English. Yes. Karadzic and Krajisnik, on the 7th of August. And then on page 2 I am saying all of these things in relation to the agreement. And around the middle of the page I say: "I think that our 'hawks' can be sorry that they also went. There are some of 'our' people --" Yes, it's the second page in Serbian, as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see where you're -- oh, I see it now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Below Zulfikarpasic you see the quotation marks: "'Our' people who say, well, let them start," and then there is some profanity, "so that we can finish it once and for all." So I am quoting our hawks. And Krajisnik says, "Yes." "For all time," says Karadzic. "So many of our 'own' people will be disappointed if we reach an agreement with the Muslims." Krajisnik says, "You know, what they're saying. Our hawks will not agree with that for sure." And I say, "They will not agree. They won't." And then English page 4 and page 3 in Serbian. English page 4, Serbian 3: "We don't want to fight with you any more. If you leave, we are going to vote against, but we are not going to fight any more." And up here it says that, "We are reaching an agreement with Adil, and we are getting -- taking care of our business. We have other things to do. So as for departures from Yugoslavia, our attitude is we're not going to fight if somebody wants to leave but we are going to vote against it." Can you see that line?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Serbian it's six from the bottom, and in the English it's the first line from the top.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I see -- I do see that line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that not confirm our position that it is necessary to vote but not to wage war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm -- without reviewing this further, and I'm a little bit uncertain about the flow of the conversation, I -- I don't know whether this is another one of those anodyne statements that is put out for good measure or whether it may refer to the specific situation in one part of Bosnia or even part of your, sort of, effort to re-centralise the SDS, I agree that's what it says here, but I'm just not able to give it much more context -- or any context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the context is what recedes it, the preceding sentence, the same document, that our hawks, because the Muslim hawks, too, see it says that up here, or, rather, on the previous page, on page 2 in English. The SDS won't say anything. Nikola tells me that Filipovic was even more convincing on Belgrade TV that he presented 100 arguments, I mean arguments in favour of the agreement. And then further down I say that I understand them because our hawks would be opposed to the agreement too. And then towards the end I say that our position is that we are going to vote against it but we're for the going to fight with anyone. Do you see the context now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, do I see some further context now. I see the very top of the page here in English, "Tunjo," which is a reference to Filipovic, said that he would have 40 per cent in new elections, he said, of the Muslim votes. And that's his use of this potential agreement to try to get -- ratchet up the position of his small party in any future balloting. So I think it is, indeed, an effort that you're promoting to make anybody who opposes this agreement look like a war monger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D276, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you, Professor, that I am now dealing only with traces or, rather, evidence pertaining to the state of mind in view of war and peace.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 30161 is the 65 ter number I'd like to have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telephone conversation between Nenad Stevandic, a young student of medicine then at the time, and Karadzic on the 18th of August. So all of this is in August. Serbian page 2, English page 1 for the time being. It says here: "Tell them not to do anything stupid." English page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page. Bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Tell them," yes: "Tell them not to do anything stupid on any account, because then we would be accused of these stupidities. Alija, and tell them this outright. Alija, remember this, does not have any arguments against the Serbs. He cannot tell the Muslims we don't want to reach an agreement with the Serbs. However, he cannot say why it is that we don't want that." So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait. We need to see the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he says to the Muslims, "We don't want to reach agreement with the Serbs," but he cannot say why. So we shouldn't provide him with any arguments. Don't you see that I am asking this young man to use his influence so that nothing stupid is done and not to strengthen that line within the Muslim leadership that is opposed to the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I take it somewhat differently. The -- it seems to me you're dealing here with -- you're struggling to deal with the leadership of the Bosnian Krajina, the ZOBK, the Community of Municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, who had been, in a sense, brought to heel in the wake of the proclamation of the unity of the two Krajinas in late June with a decision reached at that meeting that you reference where you gave the speech on St. Peter and Paul's day to put all regionalisation under the Main Board, and that had evoked a series of efforts, threats, if you will, by the leadership of the Bosnian Krajina to declare a separate polity of some sort there. So what's going on here, I think, is that you're trying to use this young medical student who -- I don't know if he -- I don't know if he held any political position, but to try to use them to keep these people in -- in Banja Luka in line, keep them quiet until the agreement is signed, which you anticipated, I believe, would be signed very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For your information, this young man was a member of the committee of the Serb Democratic Party in Banja Luka and in Krajina, and he was against any breakups that contribute to tensions. So you felt this right. I am asking him to prevent hotheads from making mistakes. And now let's move on to page 2. In Serbian it's still page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please do not make statements without asking the witness. Dr. Donia, would you like to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. That's my understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 2 in English, please, and then Radovan Karadzic says: "Yes. Therefore, why would we help him now find his way? Let him sink. Zulfikarpasic is trying to send him as well and everybody else. He has to tell the Muslims why he wants war against the Serbs. He has to explain that. And now if they do something stupid there he's going say this is why we want war against the Serbs. That is along the lines of what we were saying a few moments ago; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of it. I think the effort here is to undermine Izetbegovic, try to enlist this young man and painting him as a war monger and to use the prospect of the -- giving him an occasion or a pretext for turning away from the agreement to calm the -- those Serbs in the Bosnian Krajina leadership who were making noises about autonomy of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, do you agree that I don't want to undermine Izetbegovic? I'm just talking about the possible alibi he might have for waging war against the Serbs or how he could explain things to the Muslims, why he wanted to wage war against the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think this is part of the overall effort to undermine Izetbegovic and to force him, basically, to concur in this agreement by working against him with both Muslims and Serbs who were similarly inclined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be admitted as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D277, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now have 30242, 65 ter number. Could I now please have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, this is a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Vojo Kupresanin on the 18th of September, 1991, as we can see on page 1, and then Serbian page number 3 and English page number 2. Radovan Karadzic is advocating the following here: That reservists should respond to the JNA call-up. And we're going to see now why it is that I'm saying that. I am saying that this has proven to be the case now. They should all urgently go to the local boards. Mass response, because whether there will be war or peace depends on that. Again there's a profanity there. Let me respond. The barracks should be brought up to normal levels. And then further down, yes, yes, yes. Let the barracks be as full as possible. Let there be this army replenishment so that we can show and prove to Europe that peace is the only way out, that they should not wage war. Can't you see that we are advocating mobilisation in order to avert the danger of war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this goes to the fundamental decision that was made sometime in 1990, or maybe earlier, by President Milosevic that the Serbs should not organise their own army, that they should instead support and join the JNA in accord with various call-ups and mobilisations in order to retain for the Milosevic regime and its allies the services of the JNA as by far the most significant military force in the region. Now, I think that was a fateful decision, because it meant that -- it put the JNA in the position of supporting the various Serb political movements outside of Serbia proper. And so this to me is absolutely in accord with your position on -- on that, which was you wanted to prevent the leaders in the Bosnian Krajina from organising a separate Serb army, and in this situation, specifically you wanted to prevent them from marching off on their own into Croatia in support of the Serbian uprising there -- or Serb fight with the -- with the Croatian security forces. And that became a huge issue at this time, and it was absolutely essential for you, both at Milosevic's behest and to keep your own control over the party in that area --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, Dr. Karadzic. Don't -- you interrupted Dr. Donia's response in a different manner. Please continue. Please concentrate on the doctor's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I think this -- this intercept is really, to me, a very appropriate illustration of the position that you were in right then, and that's why I will certainly agree with the statements you made about peace. I'm not too sure it makes sense to say that we're going to mobilise and add a bunch of soldiers and thereby increase our military preparedness in order to -- because we're so committed to peace, but those are your words here. And again I don't accept them as a broad, general statement of your peaceful intentions for all time and eternity, but I certainly accept them as a statement of your policy at this point, which was you didn't want these people to be marching off on their own into Croatia and adding to the difficulties of working with the JNA in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do agree, don't you, that in mid-September the JNA was a legal and legitimate military force and that -- the fact that we advocated response to mobilisation also meant that we opposed paramilitary formations, which is something that you said as well. Now, tell me, please, was the JNA at that point in time a legitimate military force in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It may have -- it was engaging in some activities at that time which some people in Bosnia believed were not legitimate and legal, but as a whole, as a force it was indeed the Yugoslav People's Army and therefore a legitimate military force in all republics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted, please, in the regular way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D278, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call 65 ter 30335.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an intercept of my conversation with a writer, Gojko Djogo, and this conversation is known. It is quite complicated, and we will now only deal with the page that speaks of the war. So could we have page 2 both in English and in Serbian. And to avoid me reading this, would everybody please look at the portion where I say, "At the Assembly." "At the Assembly Alija Izetbegovic spoke two or three times," and then I go on to say what I said, how we are allowing them to do that. So I'm informing my friend Djogo about what we were doing at the Assembly and how we were trying to avert the war and how they would fare well, fare badly should there be a war, and that -- how they should be beaten if they initiate the war and how they would disappear, disappear from the face of the earth if they continue with these efforts and that they were offered more than the Serbs had ever been offered, and that they should go to the Assembly of Yugoslavia if they wanted to achieve that, because there was no chance of them achieving that here. So do you remember that we established that the Federal Presidency adopted the procedure for seceding from Yugoslavia and that it was done in a constitutional manner in the Assembly of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, how can you cite this intercept and these few words about peaceful intentions without following it with the context of what you portrayed as this apocalyptic destruction of the Serb people -- or of the Muslim people? That is -- is to me the most -- you can't be indifferent to the fact that you first offer up these nice little comments about the desire for peace then and go into this wildly imagined destructive scenario which would seem to just push aside any significance one would attribute to the earlier comments in your -- in your remarks here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will qualify this later, but let us look now at what I uttered. This intercept is frequently quoted as detrimental to me, and now I am putting it before all of us. I say we are allowing them to do this. However, they are preparing to wage the war, and they will try to start a war. So the topic is war and peace. And in the middle of the second page I say we are allowing them. We are allowing them to do what they want. And then Djogo says at the top, "Gentlemen, you are doing what you want." And then I say we are allowing them, and then towards the bottom I am telling them that they should go to the Assembly of Yugoslavia, to seek a constitutional manner of seceding from Yugoslavia. And it is true that I anticipated that should there be a war they would fare the worst, and that's how it was because they went to war against the Serbs and the Croats and everybody else. So why do you think that I'm wishing for this? I'm simply warning that this is how it could be. Am I wishing for war or am I trying to prevent the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you answer, Doctor, I take it that you remember the context or the contents of this intercepted conversation, because it -- because all of the parts were not shown to us now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. On that basis you may proceed to answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You speak here -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. You speak here as one who is totally in control of the situation, and you say to your interlocutor that you will allow the Muslims to take this way out, and if they don't take this way out that certain things are going to happen to them, and the certain things that are going to happen to them amount to their near total destruction. The issue of war or peace is something that you say you hold in your hands depending on how they behave. It's a clear statement in the first part of this paragraph that you just read that you are going to grant them at your largess the opportunity to do what you think they ought to do or else these consequences are going to be dire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let us be more specific. Am I saying here that they were getting ready for the war while we were proposing a political solution? Yes or no? They were getting ready for the war. They would try to wage war here. Do you see that on page 2 in the English version?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying that, "We let them, but they are preparing for war." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And previously, Djogo says let them do what they want, and I'm saying we are letting them doing what they want, but they do not want to go to the Assembly. Rather, they're getting ready for the war. So I'm not controlling anything. I'm just saying that they were getting ready for the war, and should there be a war there could be a catastrophe. And let me ask you this: You didn't know this on the first day. Did the Presidency of Yugoslavia adopt a methodology for legal and constitutional manner of seceding from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Doctor, would you agree with the observation of the accused in interpreting that "we let them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have a somewhat different interpretation of it, but they are his words, and I'm not too sure that I would -- well, I can't -- I can't, you know, speak for what was in his inner heart at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed to answer. Thank you. To his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. The question then is did the Presidency of Yugoslavia adopt a methodology. I don't know that. My recollection of the other day was that there was a -- you suggested there was a proposal entered but not -- not adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, with that we'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we're still dealing with this document. Could we now see page -- this is an intercept that I think you're aware of, Mr. Donia, because the indictment relies on it heavily. Djogo and I are talking here, and we are anticipating various difficult scenarios. Now I would like us to turn to page 8 in English. Page 8 in English, and 228 in Serbian. So five pages down. I here speak of Faletici, and I say tonight they fired at a warehouse near Sarajevo, the Muslims did. And then Djogo says where? And I say in Faletici, just above the Old Town however, the warehouse is completely mined and they can only take a very narrow path to past. And then I say that it is completely clear, that even the MUP works against the army, and they know exactly who in the MUP is doing that, and they are following the movements of the army and making assessments and on. They were preparing. They did had some weaponry. The MUP distributed the weapons to them. And we said to Izetbegovic we don't mind that the Muslims having weapons, although we hope that you're not crazy enough to use weapons against the Serbs, and it will be difficult for the Serbs but you will see how they will fare. You don't stand a chance. Dissociate yourselves from the Ustashas and have your own policies and mind your own business. So you see here that I said I didn't mind the Muslims getting weapons if they wanted to defend themselves. Do you remember me stating this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the passage from my earlier review of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember me stating in the media, publicly, that we didn't mind the Muslims arming themselves if they were procuring weapons in order to defend themselves? We didn't mind them getting weapons, as long as they were not going to attack us with those weapons.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see page 9 in English. I go on to say, "But we still have negotiations scheduled for tomorrow." We have negotiations tomorrow, and we will try to come up with an option which would be acceptable to everybody. That we had nothing against them separating out their own areas, but what will they do with that? They can't do anything with that. They can only have a somewhat greater autonomy and so on. And then below that I say they have no way of carrying out a secession. I think that this is clear to everybody, including the army. It will be a bloody slaughter, and on this occasion the army will not use only two planes. So that's page 9. And then if we can see page 12 in English. Do we have page 12? Where I say: "They, because you really can't -- you want really say that there aren't any. There are some ordinary people out there, and I think that we should stretch out both arms to them, but as far as the leadership is concerned, there is no hesitation there. They have to know that if they want to secede, they will have to start a war against us and beat us, fight us, and then we will respond back. That goes without saying." Do you remember that we were saying that we had what we needed in Bosnia-Herzegovina? We had our territory. We had had our power, and if they wanted to declare a state of their own, they couldn't do that in our territory. Do you remember us saying that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what you're saying here is what I characterise as the -- as part of -- closely related to the disappearance diatribe which is what you engage in in this intercept as a whole and indicate that the Muslims have only a couple of options. You determine what is successful or what is acceptable for the options that they can pursue, and if they choose to pursue other options or don't comply with your conditions that there will be this war, conflagration that will result in their disappearance. And this is, I think, language that you -- I first encounter at -- in a telephone conversation that you had with -- intercept that you had with Mr. Krajisnik on the 4th of September in which he cautioned you, he coached you in a sense, against using this type of language, and he said be sure that you use -- when you use this, say, Hey, we're all going to disappear. He said that to you, and you essentially disregarded his advice. And in a number of subsequent telephone conversations, and this is one of them, continued to use the formulation that the Muslims would disappear. The Muslims would be the primary losers in any conflict. And then, you know, you further allowed that same language to creep into the last few sentences of your public speech to the Assembly session on the 14th, 15th of October. So the language here, to me, is clearly a one that is threatening and one that is directed against the Muslims whom you now have given just a few options which if they don't take terrible Draconian -- horrific things are going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, by using those threatening words as you call them, am I talking them into a war or am I trying to talk them out of going to war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that have you were -- and just to note that in this case you're not talking to them in this conversation, but use of the language in general contributed to heightened tensions and certainly made them more inclined to prepare for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that somebody had a right to impose a solution to Serbs? Do you think that somebody had a right to change the position of the Bosnia and Herzegovina in an unconstitutional way and that we were duty bond to accept that? Please answer with yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you've asked that question a number of times before and I think I have indicated at that time I can't sort out constitutional issues in the departure of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the federation. Whether it would be constitutional or not, I don't know. Whether there would be a constitutional way to do it or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you see here, professor, we can see here that we are leaving some options for them. We have the situation we want. We are in Yugoslavia. They want to take us out of Yugoslavia in an unconstitutional way, and we are giving them several options. We are saying you can do it this way, that way, but you cannot force us. And where can you see the fault with the Serbs here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do I see the fault with the Serbs? I see the fault with you. I see the fault with your statements which are clearly threatening and clearly issued from the point of view of someone who believes he has command of the situation and can dictate to the Muslims what their options are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Donia, you will see now that I'm saying that I could accept that the things would go their way and that there was no chance. Did you see that in other intercepts, even the one with Mr. Zepinic, as well as this one with Mr. Djogo? I'm saying to everybody that regardless of what I would accept, there would be chaos. A chaos would ensue in Bosnia-Herzegovina in two hours. Do you think that I could control 2 million Serbs who would rebel against this attempt to take them back to the Turkish times?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do I believe you had sufficient control of the SDS and the broader Serb followers of the party to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now see page 7 of this document in English. Page 7 in English. "No, they don't understand": "No, they don't understand that the Serbs are at a boiling point, that the Serbs take time to ignite, but they burning for a long time. They don't have a clue. I can't tell our Muslim partners here," and then there's a curse. "Don't you understand that the Serbs will fight to the last man for their state so as not to lose it?" Do you remember that Zulfikarpasic said that, in the Turkish times, the Serbs and Croats were a second-rate nation and they were afraid they could become one once again? Do you remember what Zulfikarpasic said? We read that just the other day.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are here again absolutising the Serb people and assuming that they have a single will, a single wish of which you are the interpreter, and basically then opting out of your own responsibility for these statements and these threats by blaming it on some inevitable response of the Serb people. I don't think that was, in fact, the case, and I stand by my point that I think this is a choice you made to express things in these terms and to invoke the imminent will of the Serb people for something that you were, in fact, responsible for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it may have been said and I may have missed it, I can see who you're speaking to here, Djogo, but what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a poet. He had no political position. He's a friend of mine. We were talking, and I explained to him what our situation was like. This is two friends talking. He held no political office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's what I thought, but I wanted to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I think that's wrong. I agree with everything you just said, but he was also president of the Association of the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Belgrade, which was -- one could consider a NGO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was a humanitarian association. They held no political power. They dealt with humanitarian issues, the association, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- I call them a NGO. I think that's essentially the same thing, but you did have him speak at a number of different SDS sponsored events, and I believe he even addressed the founding Assembly or one of the early Assemblies under the title of the president of the Association of Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But don't you agree that there were several presidents? There was Dr. Jamagija [phoen] who held that post. So it was not a political position, was it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a political position, because he used the title to express political views, and I agree fully that he was a long-time friend of you -- yours, and you'd done great things for him, and he for you, and I agree that this is a conversation between two long-time friends and therefore a very candid conversation. You, at the end, indicate best greetings to his wife and child, but he did hold a post from which he issued political opinions and did play that role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity, Doctor, how did you know that Mr. Djogo and Mr. Karadzic had been long-time friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he -- each of them, actually, have written about it in some articles that were published. There's a wonderful book which is called "Radovan," edited and gathered by a woman named Bulatovic, Ljiljana Bulatovic, which contains a whole variety of essays and a number of speeches, some of Dr. Karadzic's poetry. It's a very -- to me a very rich resource on Dr. Karadzic's life and his entry into politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Is that book published in English, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not, I'm afraid. I'd be glad to provide a copy of the book and -- for possible translation if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No. I think that would be too big a task. But the chance of me learning Serbo-Croat is so remote that I'll just leave it up to your description, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now just draw your attention to the last portion that I read out where I'm making a distinction between the people and the leadership. You know, that there are different leaderships and that I was on good terms with the MBO leadership and with Abdic. However, as far as the leadership is concerned, well, whatever, but then the Muslim -- we should put a hand out to the Muslim people -- or, rather, both hands out to the Muslim people. That's on page 12 in English. If you wish, I can read it out.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "They -- well, because you really can't, you know, you can't say that there aren't any because there are ordinary people out there, and I think that they should be welcomed with open arms, but as far as the leadership is concerned, there will be no hesitation. They must know that if they want to secede they will have to --" see so we make a distinction between the people and the leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you did this quite frequently, actually, to have very different views about the leadership, by which you meant the leadership of the SDA, and what you conceived of as a broader Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice when a Muslim intellectual, Causevic, was leaving the SDA before all the conflicts, that he said to Izetbegovic, "Do you think that the Serbs are fools and that they cannot see what you're doing?" Did you notice that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? When? I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was an open letter of Causevic to Izetbegovic, and he provided an explanation why he was leaving the SDA. "Do you think that the Serbs are fools and that they don't see what you're doing?" If you haven't seen it, never mind. I'm going to bring it one day and you'll see.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen it. I think, you know, this happened in all the national parties. In the early days there was a great deal of back and forth about who was going to be in the party and who was not, and splinter parties formed. Let's just say I would be certainly unsurprised to find that kind of a comment coming from someone leaving the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He left the party providing the explanation that Izetbegovic is pursuing the wrong kind of policy against the Serbs or vis-a-vis the Serbs. Now, that sentence itself shows that that was the reason that he mentioned; right? If that sentence is correct, would that be right then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you've got very similar or even stronger pronouncements coming outs of, you know, Mr. Filipovic or Professor Filipovic and Mr. Zulfikarpasic. Yes. These allegations that Izetbegovic were -- was -- was anti-Serb were not uncommon among people who were -- who either left the SDA or formed separate parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you notice how Zulfikarpasic explained his split with the SDA? He said -- I mean, he amnestied or pardoned the entire SDA and that's what I'm doing too. And he said that within the SDA there was a conspiratorial nucleus of the young Muslims who were doing everything behind the backs of the rest of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was again pretty routine critique coming from the MBO at that time, basically attacking Izetbegovic for any number of things amongst his policies or his -- his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For your information, you know, that I had objections against Izetbegovic for as long as this had to do with the Muslims, but do you agree that I was saying that this could not pertain to the Serbs? We were never trying to be the arbiters of what the Muslim people would be like or what Islam would be like. Our only concern was that this should not affect the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it certainly doesn't sound it from the language in the intercept that you just -- that you just -- that we have on the screen before us. I -- I have no question at all you were on good terms with Izetbegovic for a long time and that your -- even as your differences increased politically you actually stayed on decent personal terms for some time into the -- into the conflict. After all, you saw him regularly in the course of Assembly sessions and even later on in the course of activities related to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this intercept already been admitted as a Prosecution exhibit or should we tender it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D279, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe, Professor, that I was an autocrat or do you think I was a democrat, say in the inter-party life -- or, rather, within the party of -- of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably not an either/or question. It is a question of where one is on a continuum between one and the other. I believe you really worked hard to become the -- the autocrat of the party, if you will, the SDS, and had a lot of opposition in that regard, and I thought you basically dealt with it very constructively and became a very powerful leader of the party. Now, I think any party leader is -- of any political party, democratic, communist, or any other kind, is to some degree an autocrat if he or she is to be effective. So I think that was where your -- your greatest success lay, in a sense, at acquiring power as the leader of the party. I think you later did so as a leader of the state, but I'm not -- I wouldn't say that any of that is inherently antidemocratic. It's just the way that organisations work in any society, democratic or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the stage of reaching decisions is something that requires democracy, whereas the phase of implementing decisions calls for efficacy and responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would take that as basically a statement of democratic centralism. The way decisions were made in the Communist period with a lot of open discussion and debate followed by a phase of complete consistent -- consistent implementation and intolerance of opposition to the -- the point of view that may have been defeated in the decision-making process. So that's, I think, the way that you formulate it, I would say that in general you have to execute decisions there are made democratically with some sort of executive body that does, in fact, carry out such orders, but I think the way you formulated it is, in fact, a bit closer to the specific democratic centralism that characterised the Communist period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 30414. That's the 65 ter number. Could we have that in e-court, please? Page 6 in English. The 9th of November, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's around the time of our plebiscite; right? It was in November that it took place; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9th and 10th of November; yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Vojo Kupresanin. Could I please have page 6 in English. It's fine in English. 2, 4, 6. Six would be right in Serbian as well. Now, this is -- well, this is how it starts well, "Britain," there's a reference to Britain, and towards the middle it says: "The Serb Assembly passed a decision Saturday and Sunday from 7.00 to 1900 hours. There is no person who can change it, neither Karadzic nor Milosevic nor God himself. From 7.00 until 1900 hours that is what the Assembly decided. That Assembly where he and Vukic are members, must be respected by everybody in some way, it is the only way." And then one answer further down: "If the Assembly makes a decision then who am I to change it? I am but the a small pawn serving the Assembly and the entire Serbian people. I am not some kind after big shot or a boss who could change things. Neither is he. None of us are. We are here to serve that Assembly." See? That's the authority I have. It has to do with implementation, not with a passing of decisions. On the other hand, don't you see that we are saying that the Serb Democratic Party is not making decisions but seeking solutions? Did you not notice that even Mr. Krajisnik always asks for unanimity? If there is one person against something, he asks for things to be changed so that decisions would be unanimous. Do you agree that decision-making was very long and painstaking in our situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the pattern was that the debates were very long and painstaking and sometimes quite -- quite contentious, but the actual votes were almost always unanimous, and so I kind of took that as an indication of your authority as head of the party and enforcing party discipline when actual votes were taken as opposed to the discussion which seemed to be free-wheeling exercise in speech, including some speech that was very critical of you and critical of Milosevic, critical of Mr. Krajisnik. So it was -- it was indeed a pretty free-flowing debate. The decisions, however, almost always unanimous or very close to unanimous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you notice that every decision was invariably changed during the course of the debate and ultimately a decision would be reached that would be almost unanimous? You mentioned one example when -- when Krajisnik asked one MP, Why are you against that? And then finally when the decision changed then it was unanimous at the end; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did give that example. And I think that's a pretty good instance for the drive for unanimity in -- in decision-making. The problem, of course, was at that point, specifically to that example, was that that session is the one which so totally frustrated Mr. Krajisnik that he abruptly dismissed the session, stormed out, and a deputy chair then took over the session and resumed the -- the deliberations and the decision-making, and you and he spoke that evening of your respective frustrations with this wide open democratic procedure, and I think you proposed that it be brought more under the guidance that would be offered by various ministers of the government in the making so that they would prepare proposals in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's the way things are done otherwise, right, that the government sends proposals to the Assembly and the Assembly takes a stand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this intercept being admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D280, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 31839. That's the 65 ter number. I'm afraid we're not going to have a translation, but I'm going to deal with it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation between Miodrag Simovic, the deputy prime minister, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether Ms. Edgerton and Mr. Reid could help us again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sure we'll be able to but not immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're still dealing with the subject of my attitude towards responsibility, towards duty, and towards democracy. For example, here on page 1, 2, 3, towards the bottom of page 3, I am expressing my dissatisfaction with what Vito is doing on his own, Vito Zepinic, that is. And I'm saying to Simovic this is not a private thing. I asked 50 people about Simovic, and they said that he was excellent. Simovic was chosen, and then Simovic would be deputy prime minister. "You're not my cousin, and I had no private reason whatsoever to appoint you. We have been assured of the kind of person you are." So this is the bottom of this page. You can read your language, can't you? I asked 50 people about Simovic, and they said Simovic is excellent, and that is why Simovic was chosen. I didn't even know him. Can we look at page 2 now. It says "Yes," that's what it says on page 2, "Yes," it's towards the bottom or, rather, towards the middle, and then what is it that I'm saying? Well, the last sentence: "Well, I'm not pursuing Serb policy from my very own head. I am convening elders here. I am convening the academy of sciences in order to ask questions and present my ideas." Did you know that my -- that our political council was on very good terms with intellectuals, with top scientists, scholars, everybody that -- actually, we had a lot of them in our own ranks too.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's -- if you're asking a question about the -- the political council, you refer here to the academy of sciences and say that you convene it or call it. I think actually you appointed a few members of the academy of sciences of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the political council, and some -- some of them were, I think, you would say, avid supporters of the ideas that you expressed and provided some good council along the way. Others fell off from your policies at various times, including the actual chairman, Slavko Leovac, who remained in Sarajevo during the siege and renounced your policies in August of 2000 -- or 1992. So I agree. There was a, let's say, group of prestigious intellectuals that were appointed to the political council and some of them came from the academy of sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I use the academy here as a metaphor. You will agree with that. I'm talking about convening the elders. You agree? I mean, I use this as a metaphor. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For your information, Professor Leovac, the late Professor Leovac stayed on in Sarajevo for a while but he managed to get to Belgrade. However, he never distanced himself from us. He did criticise us, but he never -- he never denounced us or renounced us. He stayed by us and our policy. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Everybody knows that I'm right, all of those who are familiar with our situation. Professor Leovac was a great friend of ours, and since he was an elderly gentleman, we listened to him, of course, and he was critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that a question, Mr. Karadzic? Don't make a statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The question was: Is that right? At the end I meant to say, "Isn't that right?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that you listened to him in the -- in the period that we're talking about roughly here in the fall of 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, can this be admitted, this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection, of course, on the basis that this is a contemporaneous statement but just to note that the question, the initial question that was asked by Dr. Karadzic to begin this line of questioning had absolutely no relation to the passage from the intercept that he read out in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification. Thank you for your observation, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D281.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was part of the intercepts that could illustrate my attitude towards the passing of decisions and the implementation of decisions. Probably I put questions that went sort of left and right and centre. Now, Professor, do you agree that we briefly deal with a topic called regionalisation? Let us see how the topic evolved mentally and politically in Radovan Karadzic's activities. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I would hope in the course of that we would also examine the section of my excerpts report which is entitled "Regionalisation" to see the various statements there that you made as a part of my report. This is the excerpts report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if we get enough time, you are indeed one of the most important witnesses in this case. We are going to put things in context and shed a great deal of light if we're given enough time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 065 -- 457. That's the 65 ter number I'd like to have now, please. 06457.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I inform you that these are statements of some of the presidents of different parties? There's Izetbegovic. There's Karadzic. There's several of them you will see. Yes. This has been translated, the part that -- actually, it's my statement that was translated. The 26th of July is the date. The 26th of July, 1990. That is two weeks after the Serb Democratic Party was established; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally established, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Current municipal regionalisation: "The Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina are not happy with it. It does not pertain to regionalisation from the point of view of exercising national rights but from the point of view of development." Can you see the sentence? The Serbian text: "[In English] The Serbian people are not satisfied with --" [Interpretation] Toward the middle of the medium, the middle of the page: "[In English] The Serbian people are not satisfied with the current municipal organisation. This is not only the regionalisation from the aspect of realising national rights but also from the developmental aspect." [Interpretation] Do you agree that we put this forward quite early as our platform, as our legitimate right, for this to be considered?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Oslobodjenje" is a kind of newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was the -- basically the newspaper of the city of Sarajevo, and at this point a very -- very fine newspaper, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D282, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 65 ter 1 -- rather, 31793. In English page 2, and in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this in passing: Did you hear that Vojvodina gained financial independence and a greater right to use its revenues, that it was just a recent development? Did you hear of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at what I said. It says that I said: "We have to prepare legal regulations so that the regions can decide how to use their money and to send to the republic a certain portion for its needs." And then further down it says: "We will give it -- they will give it to the republic but not so that we get back 18 dinars out of hundred." This is the objection they had in Krajina, that they would give hundred dinars to the republic out of which 18 would be returned back to them for their needs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the socialist state this is what the system was? Everything would flow to the republic and then the republic would distribute it as it wanted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not a very accurate characterisation of how things worked. The communities -- I'm sorry, the communities of municipality did, in fact, exercise some financial role, but their functions were very limited, and as I said before, limited to things like sewer, water supply, in some cases education. The mantra that all the people used when this was being debated in 1991 was that they were for cultural and economic and information purposes. Those three were characterisations of the function of the communities of municipalities. The municipalities themselves were a primary source of income, tax revenues, if you will, and -- although they were regulated by the -- by the republic, were always generating much of their own income. This number of 18 out of after hundred dinars is a -- I mean, it's -- it's a fantasy. There's no kind of evidence as -- as Mr. Jaksic said in April of -- or March or April of 1991, there are no numbers to support these allegations of wily discriminatory distribution of revenues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree, don't you, that Mr. Jaksic, who was not a member of the SDS, advocated greater decentralisation on financial matters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly he did, yes. He was, in a sense, the principal architect of that argument and proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that he had nothing to do with the Serbian Democratic Party, that he had been advocating this a long time before that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that he had nothing to do with the SDS. He became, I think, a working ally of the party in this period, but I think he had been advocating these views for some time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have page 3, please, in English. As for the Serbian, we can keep the current page. And I say here it would be good if we could speed this up so that the region feels that they can use their money as they want so that the cultural life can start developing. And then further down I say at the level of the municipality, everything that is at the level of the municipalities, libraries and so on; and at the level of region, would be what belongs to the region, theatre and so on. And then a further line down that the funds would go back to them or, rather, remain with them so that they can use them as they want so that they could send it to the republic. That's democracy. There's no longer this socialist redistribution where one entity collects everything and then distributes as it pleases. So this is what the system was previously, that one entity would collect all the funds and then redistribute it, whereas our democratic proposal was that the smaller units at the lower level would collect revenues and then send it up. Do you remember that that was the difference between our democratic proposal and the old system? And this is what I say here, that this socialist redistribution system was something different. Do you agree that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I -- I'm not sure of the date of this intercept, and it may not be all that important, but it -- I'd like to see when it is, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June. We can see that on the first page. I am talking to Momir on the 8th of June, and I think that this is the late Momo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did in the hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was also -- who was the director of the Bosnia-Herzegovina bureau for protection of monuments and so on. So he was -- he worked in the cultural sphere. So do you agree that there is a difference there? One system is if the republic collects the funds and then sends it back, and the other democratic system was for municipalities to collect revenues and then send them up.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say you're espousing this viewpoint is a very sanitised way of describing what was then going on in the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities where the board was finding different ways to cut off all financial support to the central government and seizing economic assets that were within the territory that it claimed to be a part of. It is indeed the case that this was a part of your original concept as you've described it here, but the reality on the ground by that time was very different. The Bosnian Krajina was, in fact, moving forward with seizing assets and seizing power in that part of the republic in ways that didn't have much to do with these very genteel sounding measures that you suggest here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you tell us the last name of this gentleman again for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momir Jungic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Donia, on the 8th of June, what you have just described still hadn't materialised. I think that at that point even Slovenia was still paying federal taxes. And then if you remember, Slovenia stopped paying them and then Croatia followed suit, whereas Krajina didn't do it until 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the 8th of June 1991. That's -- that's false. The Krajina was -- as I say, these board meetings are -- the minutes of the board meetings are available for inspection, and as soon as the association was formally established on the 25th of -- of April, the next board meetings dealt with exactly these topics that I've indicated, as well as the recruitment of large numbers of people from these municipalities to fight with the JNA in Croatia. It also happens to be the day that the Serbs from Croatia launched an incursion, an armed incursion, into Bosnia and enter the town of Drvar and were greeted there by the SDS mayor. So this was a hot topic, if you will, the efforts that were being made to weaken or cripple and challenge the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a part of the regionalisation strategy or what I've called the municipal strategy of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Donia, that even now there is a struggle going on to return the property back to municipalities so that they can have control of them as is the case elsewhere in Europe and that our municipalities to this day do not have their own property, whereas previously they used to have it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the case. What you're saying is they had them under socialism, and then in the course of the seizure of these assets by various political formations they lost that property and restitution of that property has been a long, slow, difficult process, I think, not only in Bosnia but elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. On page 2, the first lines that I read out, I'm talking to this gentleman on the phone, and he's the director of the bureau for protection of monuments, and then I say we have to prepare the regulations, the legislation, we in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the joint Assembly, because we still had the joint Assembly, so that the regions could control their own money rather than everything going into the same centre and then being redistributed. So what I'm telling you that on the 8th of June, 1991, we still have the joint Assembly. A director of one of the joint institutions is talking to me about how to advance the development of cultural sphere in the regions, and I'm suggesting that the regions should be given a certain amount of power. And you see here that we are discussing it in economic and cultural terms, not in any national terms. And this was back on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and prior to that, in early April, the Assembly actually suspended its session while it asked the people who were forming the community of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina to, in fact, submit their proposal to the Assembly so that the Assembly could regulate this process, and the SDS opposed that and instead proceeded unilaterally as a single-party project with the opposition of the other national parties and people like Milorad Dodik, who were in the opposition parties, to form the association outside of any regulated process of rules or guidelines from the Assembly. I -- I only can look at these submissions of yours, here statements to your interlocutor as disingenuous because you had the opportunity to do exactly what you're proposing here a month before and had passed on the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not how it was, Professor, and you will see that later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence, please? And we will get to what you said about what was going on in the Assembly. We're see what the Assembly in Bosnia-Herzegovina said. Is this intercept admitted just like the others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some -- I'm telling you again, Mr. Karadzic, to refrain from making such comments at the end of the questions and answers: "That's not how it was, Professor. And you will see that later." You are not giving evidence. That statement is totally unnecessary. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D283, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, but Professor Donia is giving broad answers to narrow questions and I cannot leave it without a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter 6225.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Mr. Donia, you know, what the Assembly adopts, legislation, resolutions, declarations, constitution, decisions, conclusions and recommendations, and there is a hierarchy there, and recommendations come at the very bottom of that hierarchy; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly know that there's a hierarchy. I'm frankly not certain exactly what it is, but I don't have any reason to doubt that it -- that recommendations are at the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether it has been translated. It is possible that it has. So the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 18th of April. And here the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina recommends to the municipalities to refrain from adopting decisions on regionalisations or joining into associations of municipalities. So they did not ban them from doing that. They did not condemn them for doing that. They simply recommended. And this is the mildest form of intervention on the part of the Assembly. There is no milder intervention than this. Can you read this? So they adopt this recommendation, and then they go on to explain what the recommendation is about. If you want, I can read it: "The Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina here recommends to the Municipal Assemblies to stop adopting decisions on regionalisation or, rather, on joining the association of municipalities until the negotiations on resolving the constitutional crisis and future constitutional order of Yugoslavia is discussed in negotiations." So they did not ban it. They simply recommended that this is what the municipalities should do.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be adopted, please, this cover page of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection, but we were never notified on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your explanation, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia mentioned that the Assembly challenged it, and I had to put this forward. This document was initially placed on the OTP list, so I thought there was no need to put them on notice. This is 65 ter 6225. And otherwise, I wouldn't offer this into evidence unless -- but then Mr. Donia spoke about the regionalisation and what his position was about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's carry on. We'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D284, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the indulgence of interpreters and court reporters, I wonder if we can carry on until 2.00. If it is okay with you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour, just on this last document, since this is something that we'll have to do, perhaps we can be guided as to what should be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only that item. Do we need other things? This is, given that this is an Official Gazette, what we need is the only relevant part. The entire part that contain the part referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's passage number 120, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that is the case. It is item 120, Mr. Karadzic? Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I agree to work until 2.00. Could we have 65 ter 30045. And just very briefly let us see what Brdjanin and Karadzic say about this same aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here, "Very well ..." Karadzic says: "Tell me, please, you need to prepare. Have you already done this? You need to address the cultural fund. I think that is the most realistic option now." Brdjanin says, "Okay." Karadzic says, "So that the fund for culture is established and so that the money is channeled from all municipalities that join the regional fund and then the regional fund would send the money up to the republic for the republican institutions that you all agree on." So this was a consistent position whereby we advocated that the funds be sent to the republic but only those funds that belong to the republic and then that was in the interest of municipalities and the associations of regions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this shows the cultural funds to be an innovation, that is, it's yet to be established, and it takes money from those municipalities that joined the region and then decides for what purpose and how much to forward to the republic. This suggests to me it's just part that have process of relocating power in the region and taking it from the central government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that previously we said that municipalities should have libraries, but not every municipality can have a theatre. And then an association of municipalities can have a theatre, whereas a republic would have even more institutions. So a municipality can fund a library, but not every municipality can fund a theatre; right? And that was our motive, namely that an association of municipalities could have a theatre, whereas the republic would have more institutions because it would receive its portion, what was allocated to it, from regions and municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I indicated yesterday the motive that drove you and Mr. Kupresanin to create this thing. He expressed it pretty clearly at the time. You expressed it quite clearly in -- in retrospect in July of 1992. And I certainly don't blame you for cutting me off from reading paragraph 179 of my excerpts report, because you would certainly not want to hear your own words refute this very benign hypothesis that you're putting forth here about your own motivations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, my thesis is as follows: Had Bosnia remained in Yugoslavia, this is where it would end. Regions would be a bit more independent and they would have control over their funds. Nothing else would have happened. That was the agreement reached with Zulfikarpasic; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have you've just switched time zones a bit. We're talking about April -- we have been talking about April of 1991, by which time -- or let's say by May the process of using the regional association, in particular Bosnian Krajina, to cripple the government of Bosnia was well underway. It certainly was not irrevocable. It could have been reversed had certain agreements been reached. In fact, that was the first message that Mr. Milosevic delivered to Zulfikarpasic in Belgrade. He said, We've just been doing this to -- that is regionalisation, We've just been doing this to pressure the Muslims and we're prepared to call it off if you demand that we do so and we come to an agreement. So you -- you may, in fact, be right about that, but make no mistake about where things were as of May and June of 1991. The association was -- of communities and municipalities was being used specifically to seize economic assets, to tighten its authority, increase its authority in the region, seize gas stations, a relay tower, and promulgate regulations in general to consolidate authority at the expense of the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence and can we have 1D01355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D285.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D01355. That would be the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, I noted, if I may, you were sometimes distracted by the demeanour of the accused consulting his legal advisor, but please bear in mind you are answering the question to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also apologise, but believe me that I'm following the transcript and listening at the same time. So first and foremost, I care about hearing properly: Can we see this call to non-Serb municipalities, under quotation marks, to join up.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just note I know you have that ability to multitasks and believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this call to non-Serb municipalities to join in as well? That is the part that has been circled. No. No. The other part that is marked. Can you please go back to where you were. Yes. Right. That's it. You see the one that's marked red, and can you enlarge the last paragraph. In English it's page 2. English, page 2.
